ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Vital signs are quick, bedside checks that reveal a patient’s physiological status. They guide clinical judgment, help spot deterioration early, and inform treatment priorities, especially where resources are limited.

b: Temperature: body heat regulation
Pulse: cardiac output and rhythm
Respiration: gas exchange and ventilation
BP: perfusion and vascular tone
SpO2: oxygenation
sections.p: Vital signs—temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation—provide a snapshot of cardiovascular, respiratory, and thermoregulatory function. They are the first line of assessment in any clinical encounter.

b: Temperature rises with infection or inflammation; drops with sepsis or hypothermia
Pulse rate and rhythm indicate cardiac health and autonomic balance
Respiratory rate signals metabolic demand and pulmonary pathology
BP shows systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output
SpO2 reveals pulmonary or circulatory compromise
sections.p: Each sign reflects underlying physiology and can be altered by disease, medication, or environmental factors. Recognizing patterns of change is essential for early diagnosis and intervention.

t.b: >38.3°C suggests infection; <35°C indicates hypothermia or severe sepsis
>100/min tachycardia; <60/min bradycardia; irregular rhythm signals arrhythmia
>20/min tachypnea; <12/min bradypnea; abnormal effort suggests distress
Systolic <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg indicates hypotension; high BP suggests hypertension
<94% on room air signals hypoxemia; <90% is critical

b: Triage: prioritize patients with abnormal vitals
Shock detection: hypotension + tachycardia signals early shock
Monitoring: track response to fluids, antibiotics, or oxygen
sections.p: In low-resource settings, vital signs guide triage, detect early shock, and monitor response to treatment. They are inexpensive, repeatable, and universally applicable.

b: Trend over 24 hours is more informative than a single reading
Use the lowest BP and highest HR to assess severity
sections.p: Remember the mnemonic VITALS: Temperature, Pulse, Respiration, BP, SpO2, and look for trends over time. A single abnormal value can be benign, but a cluster often indicates pathology.

b: Not measuring temperature in febrile patients with malaria can miss hypoglycemia
sections.p: Clinicians often ignore subtle changes, misinterpret normal variations (e.g., fever in malaria), or rely on a single measurement. Inconsistent technique can lead to erroneous values.
When vital signs are abnormal, targeted investigations clarify the cause and guide therapy.

t.b: Low hemoglobin suggests anemia; high WBC indicates infection
Low <70 mg/dL indicates hypoglycemia; high >200 mg/dL suggests uncontrolled diabetes
Findings guide treatment of pneumonia or heart failure
Positive leukocytes or proteinuria indicate UTI or renal disease

b: Infection: give broad-spectrum antibiotics based on local resistance
Hypotension: give isotonic fluids; consider vasopressors if available
Hypoxia: administer oxygen via mask or nasal cannula
Fever: use antipyretics; treat underlying infection
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. In low-resource settings, prioritize readily available interventions.

b: Drug-induced fever vs. infection
sections.p: Vital signs can mimic other conditions: fever can be due to drug reactions; tachycardia may be anxiety; hypotension can be due to dehydration or sepsis.

b: Malaria can suppress fever response
sections.p: Certain conditions mask true values: fever may be absent in malaria; tachycardia may be normal in pregnancy; low SpO2 can be falsely normal in high altitude.

b: Severe hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg)
Respiratory distress (RR >30/min or SpO2 <90%)
Severe tachycardia (>140/min)
High fever (>40°C) with altered mental status
sections.p: Seek urgent care if vital signs indicate life-threatening instability.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever (>40°C) with altered mental status
